blocks.text: A dative bond is formed between two atoms when the shared pair of electrons is donated by one of the bonding atoms. Let us consider the example of bond formation between H₂O and a proton (H⁺). H₂O has two covalent bonds and there are two lone pairs of electrons on the oxygen atom. On the other hand, the proton is deficient in electrons. Therefore, the oxygen atom can donate its lone pair of electrons to the acceptor H⁺, and this results in the formation of a dative bond as in the following diagram (Figure 3.3(a)).

blocks.alt: Three examples of dative bond formation. (a) Water and H+; a blue curved arrow takes an oxygen lone pair to H+, and the product shows a red arrow from O to the new H. (b) CO: the 'Lewis structure' with three shared pairs, and the bond form with two lines and a red arrow from O to C. (c) O=O plus an oxygen free radical, labelled 'oxygen free radical'; a blue curved arrow shows a lone pair donated, giving ozone with O+ in the centre and an arrow to O-.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: Dative bond formation (a) oxonium (hydronium) ion, (b) carbon monoxide, (c) ozone molecule (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.3; the printed caption swaps (b) and (c)).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed caption swaps the panels, naming (b) ozone and (c) carbon monoxide; the figure and the text show carbon monoxide in (b) and ozone in (c), as captioned above.

Carbon monoxide also contains a dative bond between oxygen and carbon atoms. Oxygen shares its two valence shell electrons with the carbon atom to make a normal double covalent bond. However, the valency of carbon is not satisfied with these bonds. It needs one more pair of electrons to complete its octet. Oxygen atom donates one of its lone pairs for the formation of a covalent bond, which is a dative bond as exhibited in Figure 3.3(b).

The structure of ozone molecule is presented in Figure 3.3(c). It is formed by a reaction between the oxygen molecule with an oxygen atom (a free radical (O)). One of the oxygen atoms in the molecule donates a pair of electrons to make a coordinate covalent bond with this free radical. Therefore, the central atom has total three bonds including a double covalent bond on one side and a coordinate covalent bond on the other. It carries a positive charge, while the oxygen atom that accepts the lone pair carries a negative charge.

blocks.prompt: a) Draw the Lewis structures of N₂ and CS₂ molecules?
blocks.explanation: N₂: :N≡N: — the two nitrogen atoms share three pairs (a triple bond) and each nitrogen has one lone pair; every atom has a complete octet. CS₂: S=C=S — carbon shares two pairs with each sulphur (two double bonds) and each sulphur has two lone pairs.

answer_figure.alt: Two rows. N₂: three shared pairs (red dots) between the N atoms and one lone pair on each N, then the line form N≡N. CS₂: two shared pairs between C and each S and two lone pairs on each S, then the line form S=C=S.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: Lewis structures of N₂ and CS₂ (electron-dot and line forms)
answer_figure.long_description: On the left is the electron-dot form, with the shared pairs as red dots; after the arrow, the same structure is drawn with lines. N₂: three shared pairs, i.e. a triple bond, one lone pair on each N, and both octets complete. CS₂: carbon shares two pairs with each sulphur (two double bonds), and each S has two lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: b) How many electrons are there in the valence shell of B in BF₃? Does it have the ability to accept a lone pair of electrons?
blocks.explanation: Boron has three B–F bonds, i.e. only six electrons; it is two short of an octet and has one empty orbital. So yes, B can accept a lone pair from another atom (it can act as an acceptor).

blocks.prompt: c) Show the formation of a dative bond between NH₃ and BF₃.
blocks.explanation: The nitrogen of NH₃ has a lone pair; the boron of BF₃ has an empty orbital. Nitrogen donates its lone pair into the empty orbital of boron: H₃N→BF₃. Nitrogen is the donor, boron the acceptor, and both now have a complete octet.
